context: The input is choices = [1, 1, 2] at indices 0, 1, and 2. “First 1” and “second 1” distinguish indices 0 and 1. The figure puts a hat on the second 1 to identify it, but both have numerical value 1. An index can appear at most once per path. Using selected to prevent index reuse still allows permutations with identical values.
description: At the top, state has three empty slots. Blue represents the first 1, teal the second 1, and purple the 2. Each of three rounds fills a slot using an unused index, giving the six leaves in the table. Leaves 3, 4, and 6 have orange borders and point to “Duplicate permutations to remove.” The table numbers leaves from left to right and uses the borders and values to match each duplicate with the permutation to keep.

frames.explanation: Ignoring the identity marks leaves only three distinct value sequences among the six leaves: [1, 1, 2], [1, 2, 1], and [2, 1, 1].
frames.title: Equal elements produce duplicate permutations

summary: Treating the two elements with value 1 as separate candidates produces six paths but only three distinct value sequences.
